item.text: {"question_id":"6B.9","answer":"During the 2023 period, the administration established or operated formal social-institutional arrangements, including IMSS-BIENESTAR rules, CONEVAL’s legally embedded measurement role, and child-protection procedures and registries. IMSS-BIENESTAR had statutory-administrative authority, defined responsibilities, professional training and supervision procedures, indicators, complaint and citizen-oversight mechanisms, auditability, and provision for external evaluation and public reporting. These passages establish formal design and intended controls, not reliable funding, effective staffing, completed audits, or demonstrated resilience. Funding remained subject to annual congressional appropriations and later modifications, while the health system’s institutional transition was associated with deteriorating access: health-service deprivation rose from 16.2% in 2018 to 39.1% in 2022, public-sector care fell, private care increased, and catastrophic health spending remained above 2018 levels. The transition also created operational and strategic challenges, and integrated state health networks were not implemented as planned because of policy changes and a new health model. Wider evidence reports austerity-related capacity loss, administrative turnover, weak institutional continuity, under-resourced victim services, limited coordination and enforceability in extraordinary mechanisms, and weakened autonomous oversight. Some social-protection and employment-service indicators were achieved, but these results were partly shared with international, subnational, or non-governmental partners and do not establish post-rule durability. The evidence therefore supports selective institution-building with formal standards and accountability architecture, but not a reliably funded, consistently professional, transparent, and resilient social-service system demonstrably capable of surviving López Obrador’s personal and political model.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0051-E002","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0051-E005","BATCH-0051-E006","BATCH-0015-E004","BATCH-0031-E019","BATCH-0052-E017"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0032-E010","BATCH-0052-E001","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0026-E006","BATCH-0018-E014","BATCH-0018-E019","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0052-E015"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence documents formal rules more strongly than actual staffing quality, funding reliability, completed audits, or institutional survival after October 2024.","Several outcomes and implementation assessments are shared with Congress, courts, subnational authorities, international organizations, World Bank or IFC-supported systems, and other partners; personal attribution is therefore partial.","The health-access outcome evidence covers 2018–2022, while the IMSS-BIENESTAR transition was formalized for 2023; policy lag, pandemic effects, measurement changes, and incomplete causal attribution remain material.","The evidence does not establish post-rule resilience or demonstrate that formal evaluation and complaint mechanisms produced effective correction."] ,"corrections_made":["Removed the unsupported characterization that IMSS-BIENESTAR’s prescribed mechanisms demonstrated reliable funding, professional staffing, transparent operation, or resilience.","Foregrounded the supplied evidence on health-system transition, worsening access, reduced public-sector care, increased private care, and implementation failure.","Recast formal rules, indicators, audits, complaints, and evaluations as design provisions rather than demonstrated performance.","Preserved selective positive institution-building while tightening attribution and causal limits."] ,"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["Reopen if verified 2023 execution data, staffing and vacancy records, audit findings, budget outturns, complaint-resolution records, or post-2024 institutional-survival evidence become available."]}
